query: What kinds of expenses tend to get declined, and does it differ by department?

per_column.name: expense_category_type
per_column.rationale: A clean expense-type categorization directly enables grouping declined expenses by kind, which is the core of the query. Values are well-grounded in short_description/ci text (hardware, cloud_service, travel all match sources), with minor edge cases like 'ISP Services' -> software_service being reasonable.

per_column.name: asset_subcategory
per_column.rationale: A finer-grained expense breakdown gives a genuine additional axis for analyzing what gets declined. Mostly sound readings (laptop, desktop_workstation, service_subscription match text); 'Miscellaneous hardware component'/'RAM Component' -> peripheral_accessory is a mild stretch but defensible.

per_column.name: asset_brand
per_column.rationale: Brand is well-extracted from text (Dell, HP, etc.) and 'Other' is an honest fallback. Only moderately useful for a decline-by-department query; brand could plausibly correlate with declines but is a secondary axis.

per_column.name: entry_generation_method
per_column.rationale: Whether an entry was manually vs auto generated is largely orthogonal to what expenses get declined. It is also not clearly derivable from the shown source text (short_description/ci); the manual/auto assignment appears asserted without visible textual support.

per_column.name: has_source_id
per_column.rationale: This merely restates presence of the existing source_id column—trivially redundant and of little analytical leverage for decline patterns. Groundedness is fine since it reflects an actual field, though the sample rows don't expose source_id to verify.

per_column.name: ci_identifier_quality
per_column.rationale: A metadata-quality flag about the ci string; marginally relevant to declines. Categorization is a plausible reading of ci text, though 'Random Access Memory Component' -> standard_model_name is questionable, weakening grounding.

per_column.name: is_premium_or_high_end
per_column.rationale: Premium tier could plausibly relate to declines (costly items rejected), giving some leverage. But groundedness is weak: 'Dell XPS 13' (a premium ultrabook) flagged false suggests inconsistent/under-supported inference from text.

per_column.name: is_new_procurement
per_column.rationale: New-procurement vs reassignment is a reasonable axis for decline analysis. However inference seems shaky: 'Provision of Services for iPod touch' -> True while 'Miscellaneous hardware component' -> False is inconsistent, and it exactly mirrors is_premium counts (445/55), raising redundancy/derivation concerns.

per_column.name: travel_context_flag
per_column.rationale: Travel-vs-not is a meaningful expense-type split that could differ by department and correlate with declines. Well grounded in text (travel keywords), with non-travel rows correctly flagged false.

judge.rationale: The strongest columns (expense_category_type, asset_subcategory, travel_context_flag, asset_brand) give genuine new axes to characterize declined expenses and cross them with department, directly serving the query. Several columns are weaker: has_source_id merely restates an existing field, entry_generation_method is orthogonal and poorly grounded, and is_premium/is_new_procurement show inconsistent, under-supported inferences (e.g., Dell XPS 13 marked not premium) with suspiciously identical distributions. Overall the added set is useful but diluted by low-leverage and partially hallucinated flags.
